item.description: President Donald Trump has intensified his calls for lower interest rates, creating a potential conflict with Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh. Trump, who previously criticized former Fed Chair Jerome Powell, has not publicly insulted Warsh but has become more vocal about his desire for rate cuts. The Fed is expected to raise interest rates on Wednesday, with market odds exceeding 90% after August inflation data showed a 3.4% annual rate, well above the Fed's 2% target. Trump has repeatedly stated that he believes rates should be lower, even suggesting they should be as low as 1% or 0.5%, arguing that high rates disadvantage the U.S. economy. His adviser, Kevin Hassett, acknowledged the president's opinion on rate decisions but emphasized the Fed's independence. The Fed faces a dilemma: hold rates steady amid rising inflation or hike rates to combat stubbornly high prices, which could anger Trump. item.description: A federal immigration officer, Christian Castro, was arrested in Minneapolis on Wednesday after being charged with assault and lying about a shooting incident that occurred eight months prior. Castro, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent, turned himself in to the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension following an outstanding arrest warrant. The incident in question took place on January 14, when Castro shot Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan national, in the leg through the door of his apartment while children were inside. Castro had initially been released on bond from federal custody in Texas, wearing a GPS ankle monitor, after an initial appearance in U.S. District Court in McAllen, Texas, on charges of lying to investigators about the circumstances of the January 14 shooting. item.description:
President Donald Trump is confronting a wave of political and institutional setbacks that are challenging his authority both domestically and internationally. The Supreme Court blocked his attempt to restrict mail-in voting ahead of the midterm elections, prompting sharp criticism from Trump toward his own first-term appointees on the bench. Meanwhile, a federal court again rejected his effort to renovate the Kennedy Center, a controversy that has drawn scrutiny over his motives and raised questions about his respect for historical institutions.
In Congress, support for Trump's agenda is fracturing. The GOP-led House voted to require an end to his war with Iran, with seven Republicans now opposing the administration's stance. item.description:
Narges Mohammadi, the Iranian Nobel Peace Prize laureate and prominent human rights advocate, spoke with CNN from Tehran after receiving a temporary release from prison. She is recovering under medical care following a serious deterioration in her health during her years behind bars. In the interview, Mohammadi discusses her new memoir, her personal experiences in detention, and the reasons she continues to speak publicly despite the risks associated with criticizing Iran’s ruling authorities.
Mohammadi has spent years campaigning for women’s rights, political freedoms, and the abolition of the death penalty in Iran. Her activism has repeatedly resulted in imprisonment and other forms of pressure from the Iranian regime. Despite those consequences, she has maintained that speaking out is a responsibility she cannot abandon. According to Psaki, the House has only been in session for 71 out of 185 weekdays since the beginning of the year, which is less than 40 percent of the time. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) canceled all remaining votes for the week, prompting Psaki to highlight Republican Congressman Thomas Massie's theory that the Republicans are avoiding a vote on eight articles of impeachment against Peter Brian Hegseth, Trump's Secretary of Defense. Massie argued that the articles accuse Hegseth of subverting the Constitution and abusing his powers as secretary of defense. item.description:
The U.S. House of Representatives has passed a bipartisan bill aimed at protecting consumers from rising electricity costs associated with data centers. The legislation, sponsored by Rep. Gabe Evans (R-Colo.) and Rep. Kathy Castor (D-Fla.), urges state utility regulators to consider federal guidelines that would require data centers to bear the increased costs resulting from their high electricity consumption.
The move comes amid growing public concern over the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure and its impact on energy prices and water usage. Data centers, which house the servers powering AI technologies, have become a focal point of voter anxiety about the influence of major tech companies and the broader consequences of AI development.

He reminded the audience that over $2 billion had already been allocated through FEMA, and additional funds would only be provided if Whatley secured victory. Trump's remarks, which included the statement, 'I'm going to get that to you, Michael. In her most famous role in 'Forbidden Planet,' Francis wore a minimalist white dress designed by Walter Plunkett, which became iconic when her character, Altaira, asked, 'What's a bathing suit?' item.title: Former Navy Personnel Plead Guilty to Distributing Fentanyl-Laced Pills to Sailors
item.description:
Two former U.S. Navy personnel, Bailey Szramowski and Kaeo Poomaihealani, pleaded guilty in federal court in San Diego to distributing counterfeit oxycodone pills laced with fentanyl to active-duty sailors aboard the aircraft carrier U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln. According to court documents and the Justice Department, one sailor who purchased pills from Szramowski died from an acute fentanyl overdose in 2023, while another was hospitalized after taking the drugs.
In December 2022, Szramowski, 29, sold 10 fake oxycodone pills to a sailor identified as A.N., who later overdosed and died while on leave in San Leandro, California. An autopsy confirmed the cause of death as acute fentanyl intoxication, with toxicology showing fentanyl and THC in his system. Ten days after that transaction, Szramowski sold three more pills to another sailor, C.L., according to court records.

item.title: Fossilized Feather in Dinosaur Droppings Offers Clues to Bird Survival After Asteroid Impact
item.description:
Scientists have discovered exceptionally well-preserved fossilized feathers inside dinosaur droppings, or coprolites, unearthed in Montana's Hell Creek Formation. The feathers belonged to a small, flightless diving bird from the extinct Hesperornithiformes group that was eaten by a predatory dinosaur, possibly a Tyrannosaurus rex, shortly before the asteroid impact 66 million years ago that triggered a mass extinction event. This discovery, published in the journal Current Biology, represents the best-preserved feather ever extracted from Mesozoic deposits and provides a rare window into a pivotal moment in evolutionary history.
The research team, led by Jingmai O'Connor from Chicago's Field Museum, found that while some feathers resembled those of modern birds with stiff, lightweight structures, others were more primitive, smaller, and fuzzier, offering less effective insulation. item.title: New Study Challenges Earth's Formation Theory, Suggesting Inner Solar System Origin
item.description: A groundbreaking study led by planetary scientists Paolo Sossi and Dan Bower from ETH Zurich has revealed that Earth formed almost entirely from material in the inner Solar System, challenging long-held theories about the planet's origin. The research, published in Nature Astronomy, indicates that Earth's building material originated from a single reservoir in the inner Solar System, with less than two percent of its mass coming from the outer Solar System beyond Jupiter. This finding contradicts previous hypotheses that suggested 6-40 percent of Earth's material came from the outer Solar System, which was thought to be necessary for explaining the presence of water and other volatile substances on Earth. The researchers analyzed isotope ratios from ten different meteorite systems, a more comprehensive approach than previous studies that typically focused on only two isotope systems. item.description: The recent erosion of parts of the Southern California coastline, exacerbated by intense waves and flooding, has reignited concerns about the safety of storing radioactive waste at the San Onofre nuclear power plant. While Southern California Edison, the plant's owner, claims the current storage system is safe for decades and has pledged to move the waste to higher ground if necessary, experts caution that long-term geological risks remain. The plant's twin domes, which housed reactor cores, will begin dismantling in early 2027, but the 3.6 million pounds of high-level waste will remain on-site indefinitely. item.description: A tragic helicopter crash occurred in Chatsworth, Los Angeles, on Tuesday evening, resulting in the deaths of NBC4 news reporter Eliana Moreno and pilot George Marciniw, along with a third person on the ground, Edy Mejia. The incident took place around 7 p.m. while the crew was covering a fatal vehicle collision involving an SUV and a Metro bus that had already claimed two lives and injured six others. Moreno, a seasoned journalist with over a decade of experience in news helicopter coverage, was known as 'Eli in the heli' on social media and had worked for NBCLA and Telemundo 52. Marciniw, a veteran pilot with more than 30 years of experience and 14,000 flight hours, was also a flight instructor. The helicopter, which was part of NBC4's aerial news coverage, crashed between two commercial buildings on Mason Avenue. item.title: Energy Price Shock's Role in U.S. Inflation Ahead of Fed Rate Decision
item.description: The Wall Street Journal's live coverage of the Federal Reserve's September 16, 2026 meeting highlights a central question for policymakers: how much of the persistent inflation pressure stems from the recent energy price shock. With crude oil prices up sharply this year and gasoline costs rising more than 27% compared with a year earlier, energy has become a dominant driver of headline inflation even as core measures remain elevated. The Fed has held interest rates steady since January 2026, waiting to gauge how tariffs and energy price swings would pass through to consumer prices. However, August CPI data showed inflation stuck at 3.4% annually, well above the Fed's 2% target, strengthening market expectations for a quarter-point rate increase—the first since 2023. Analysts note that while energy directly lifts prices at the pump and for diesel-dependent goods, its broader impact depends on how long the shock lasts and whether it spills into wages and services inflation. item.description: The Federal Reserve has raised interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point to the 3.75%-4.00% range, signaling further tightening of monetary policy in the coming months. This decision, made unanimously with new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh joining the vote, comes as inflation remains stubbornly high despite President Donald Trump's promises to lower prices. The Fed cited the combined impact of Trump's global import tariffs, an energy shock following the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran, and capital spending from the artificial intelligence boom as key factors keeping price pressures elevated. Policymakers now project 16 of 18 members anticipate at least one more rate hike by year-end, with the policy rate expected to reach 4.00%-4.25% by December. The Fed's statement dropped previous references to 'supply shocks' in the energy sector, indicating broader inflation concerns. item.description: An 18-year-old Cal State Fullerton student, Anthony Joseph Blas, died Sunday after an off-campus fraternity party, according to Fullerton police. Blas was pronounced dead shortly after being dropped off at Providence St. Jude Medical Center around midnight. The incident occurred at a fraternity function north of campus that is unaffiliated with the university. Police indicated alcohol may have been a factor in the death, though the exact cause and manner of death have not yet been determined. Blas, a recent graduate of Los Altos High School in Hacienda Heights, was accepted to 17 other universities before choosing Cal State Fullerton. The university issued a statement expressing condolences to the student's family and the campus community, offering psychological services to students. Cal State Fullerton emphasized that their hearts are with the family during this difficult time. item.title: Three killed, including news pilot and reporter, in Los Angeles helicopter crash
item.description:
A news helicopter operated for NBC4 and Telemundo 52 crashed Tuesday evening in a commercial area of Chatsworth, Los Angeles, killing three people and injuring at least two others, according to local officials. The victims included pilot George Marciniw and aerial photojournalist and reporter Eliana Moreno. A pedestrian in a nearby parking lot was also killed.
The Eurocopter AS350 was covering a fatal bus collision in Chatsworth, roughly 25 miles northwest of downtown Los Angeles, when it crashed between two commercial buildings. More than 70 firefighters responded to the scene, extinguished the resulting fire and reported damage to two storage containers and four vehicles. The helicopter, which was built in 2004 according to Federal Aviation Administration records, was described as heavily destroyed.

item.title: Pennsylvania Reports Fourth Measles Death in 2026 Outbreak
item.description:
Pennsylvania health officials announced on Tuesday that a fourth person in the state had died from measles, making 2026 the deadliest year for measles in the United States since the virus was declared eliminated in 2000. The Mifflin County coroner's office said an 18-year-old died from a rare neurological complication of measles. The person was not vaccinated, according to the state health department.
A coroner from another Pennsylvania county announced this week that a 40-year-old unvaccinated woman had died from measles complications. On Tuesday, that coroner, Greg Furlong, said that testing had confirmed the woman had contracted measles. Last month, state health officials reported the deaths of two infants who had measles.

item.title: Simulation Links Early Universe Turbulence to Black Hole Formation and Little Red Dots
item.description:
Astronomers have identified millions of black holes over the past five decades, yet the processes by which these incredibly dense entities form and evolve remain largely unknown. In a new study published in the journal Nature, astrophysicist Dr. Chon presents a simulation of the early universe that connects black hole formation with a recently identified phenomenon known as 'little red dots.'
The simulation indicates that massive black holes may naturally emerge from the turbulent flows of material present in the early universe. As these black holes rapidly accumulate this material, their light emissions resemble the little red dots that astronomers observe today using the James Webb Space Telescope.

Aaron Guckian has won the Republican nomination for governor of Rhode Island after defeating Elaine Pelino in a closely contested primary that prompted a recount request. item.title: Firefox 156 Improves Performance for Large Images and PDFs, Introduces AI Control Features
item.description: Firefox 156, the second release since Mozilla adopted a twice-monthly release schedule, introduces several performance improvements and new features. The browser now uses libjpeg-turbo's IDCT scaling to reduce large JPEG images during decoding, rather than loading full-size images and then shrinking them. Benchmarks show up to 20% less memory usage during very large image loading, with decoding up to twice as fast. These improvements are efficient behind the scenes without noticeable changes to the user experience. The built-in PDF viewer starts up to 45% faster as the browser now loads the background PDF.js worker sooner rather than launching it only when needed. Sponsored suggestions in the address bar are now live for users in France, Germany, and Italy, though these can be disabled via Settings > Search > Firefox Suggest > Suggestions from Sponsors. The company is raising the minimum starting pay to $20 per hour, with an average hourly pay of nearly $24 per hour, representing a $1 per hour increase for eligible employees. item.description: In the summer of 2018, a man hunting for mammoth ivory in northeastern Siberia discovered a remarkably well-preserved wolf head in the thawing permafrost along the Tirekhtyakh River. The head, measuring approximately 40 centimeters from nose to neck, retained its fur, whiskers, teeth, and even brain tissue, having remained frozen for roughly 40,000 years. The specimen was handed over to the Academy of Sciences of the Republic of Sakha, where director Albert Protopopov noted that while frozen wolf cubs had been found before, this was the first instance of a fully grown wolf with soft tissue intact. Researchers used CT scans to create a 3D model of the skull and brain cavity, confirming no signs of human or animal interference. The wolf was determined to be approximately 18 months old, a young adult, rather than a fully mature adult as initially believed. item.description: The article discusses a groundbreaking cancer therapy developed by researchers at the University of Adelaide, led by Professor Chunxia Zhao. The treatment utilizes 'smart' nanoparticles to deliver mRNA directly to tumor sites, specifically targeting tumor-associated macrophages that have been reprogrammed by cancer to suppress immune responses. The mRNA carries instructions for producing CXCL9, a chemical signal that recruits T cells, which are critical for attacking cancer cells. The nanoparticles are designed with antibodies that bind to TREM2, a protein found on immunosuppressive macrophages, ensuring precise delivery to the tumor microenvironment. Additionally, the nanoparticles carry resiquimod, a drug that stimulates immune pathways. item.title: Cat Frazier, Digital Artist Who Revived the Internet’s Early Aesthetic, Dies at 35
item.description:
Cat Frazier, a graphic designer and digital artist known for celebrating the colorful and eccentric visual language of the early internet, has died at age 35. Her work drew heavily on the aesthetics of websites and online platforms from the 1990s and 2000s, including GeoCities, Blingee, and MySpace.
Frazier became increasingly dissatisfied with the restrained, minimalist design principles emphasized during her studies at Pratt Institute in Brooklyn. She found the clean layouts, muted palettes, and carefully controlled typography favored by contemporary graphic design instructors and professionals too uniform and impersonal. Rather than treating those early internet styles as outdated or poorly designed, she saw them as expressive, playful, and deeply personal.

item.title: AI scribes reduce clinical documentation time by 69.1% in primary care simulation
item.description:
A study led by researchers at the University of Toronto found that artificial intelligence (AI) scribes substantially reduced the amount of time physicians spent documenting patient visits during simulated primary care appointments. The study, published in JAMIA Open, involved nine physicians who completed simulated encounters both with and without AI scribe technology. Researchers analyzed video recordings to compare how physicians allocated their time.
When AI scribes were used, physicians spent 69.1% less time on clinical documentation. Without the technology, doctors devoted more than one-third of each simulated encounter to note-taking. AI scribes instead recorded the encounter and generated structured clinical notes that physicians could subsequently review and edit. Researchers observed that this workflow reduced interruptions during patient interactions and shifted documentation activity toward reviewing and correcting AI-generated notes.

item.title: Lauren Bacall’s Iconic Legs and Screen Presence in Classic Hollywood
item.description: Lauren Bacall, a symbol of classic Hollywood glamour, is celebrated for her legendary legs, which were an integral part of her screen presence and overall image. The article highlights how her long, elegant legs contributed to her confident and sultry allure, setting her apart from other leading ladies of the 1940s and 1950s. Bacall's posture and poise, combined with her smoky voice and piercing gaze, made her a magnetic figure in films such as 'To Have and Have Not' (1944) and 'The Big Sleep' (1946). Her legs were not merely a physical attribute but a symbol of the cool, effortless sex appeal that defined her era. The article emphasizes that while her legs were a significant part of her iconic image, they were just one element of her broader legacy, which included her talent, charisma, and distinctive style. The piece is part of a blog called 'Vintage Everyday,' which features vintage photographs and stories from the 1940s and 1950s, focusing on beauty, fashion, and celebrity culture.

item.title: California and U.S. Laws Prompt New Lawsuits for Return of Nazi-Looted Art Held by Museums
item.description: Two new lawsuits have been filed in California seeking the return of artwork looted by the Nazis during World War II, prompted by recent state and federal laws that strengthen claims to such art. The first lawsuit, filed in federal court in Los Angeles, was brought by the daughters of Dina Gottliebova Babbitt, an Auschwitz survivor, against the Auschwitz-Birkenau Memorial and Museum in Poland. They seek the return of watercolors created by their mother under Nazi coercion, which she painted for Josef Mengele, the Nazi physician and war criminal known as the 'Angel of Death.' The second lawsuit, filed in Los Angeles Superior Court, was brought by the Jewish Federation of Greater Los Angeles and Daniel Gryczman against the Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena. They seek the return of the diptych 'Adam and Eve,' a 16th-century masterpiece by Lucas Cranach the Elder, which was part of a collection seized from Dutch Jewish art dealer Jacques Goudstikker by Hermann Göring. item.title: Former President Obama Honors Sunny, His Portuguese Water Dog, Following Her Passing
item.description: Former President Barack Obama expressed deep sorrow over the passing of Sunny, his family's Portuguese Water Dog and the second First Dog of the United States. In a heartfelt social media post on X, Obama shared memories of Sunny, who joined the White House during his second term in 2013. He described her as a 'force of nature' with boundless energy, often leaping over hedges on the South Lawn while chasing squirrels and birds. Obama also fondly recalled Sunny's playful quirks, such as being a 'loud and sloppy drinker' and her unusual aversion to water despite being a Portuguese Water Dog. The Obamas had previously welcomed Bo, their first dog, in 2009, who passed away in 2021. Sunny, who was with the family for thirteen years, was described by Obama as 'always loyal, always sweet, always ready for adventure.' The former president concluded his tribute by imagining Sunny reuniting with Bo, his first dog, in the afterlife. The post, which included a photo of the Obamas with their dogs,

item.title: House Bill to Release Epstein Files Gains Momentum Amid White House Concerns
item.description: A House-led effort to release more information about convicted child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein is gaining traction, according to two GOP lawmakers. The bill, a successor to the successful Epstein Files Transparency Act (EFTA), aims to force the Justice Department to release additional files that have been accused of being unlawfully withheld. The new discharge petition, filed by Reps. Thomas Massie (R-KY) and Ro Khanna (D-CA), requires 218 signatures to move forward. As of Monday night, 160 House members had signed the petition, with the 218th signature now within reach. Khanna stated that Wednesday and Thursday are the last days to sign before recess, and they need the remaining Democrats to sign to reach 217, with Massie delivering the final signature. Massie claimed that some GOP colleagues are reluctant to sign due to pressure from the White House, urging them to take credit for the bill before the election. item.title: L.A. County Restraining Order System Faces High Dismissal Rates Amid Procedural Challenges
item.description: L.A. County's domestic violence restraining order system is facing significant challenges, with only 21% of requests granted in 2025, according to a Los Angeles Times investigation. The report reveals that 57% of petitions were dismissed due to procedural delays, the highest rate in California. The process requires victims to complete multiple forms, gather evidence, serve the abuser, and attend court hearings while managing abuse and other responsibilities. Most applicants are self-represented, navigating the system without legal assistance. The Office of Violence Prevention identified 13 recommendations to improve the system, but only three have been implemented. The Times analysis also found that 63 women were killed by current or former partners in L.A. County between 2024 and 2025, with 10 of those women having filed for restraining orders. Of those, four had permanent protection granted, but three were killed shortly after submitting their requests. The Sheriff's Department has s

item.title: Tampa Bay Rays' Junior Caminero hits walk-off home run with slow trot, strengthens AL MVP case
item.description: Tampa Bay Rays outfielder Junior Caminero, a 23-year-old phenom, hit his 41st home run of the season on Tuesday night, securing a 2-1 victory over the Oakland Athletics. The walk-off home run, which came in the ninth inning, was notable not for its power but for Caminero's unusually slow trot around the bases. The slugger took approximately 40 seconds to complete his circuit, engaging in extended high-fives with teammates along the first base line. This behavior drew attention as it appeared to contradict the common practice of quickly completing the trot to avoid touching the batter before he reaches home plate. However, research revealed that MLB has no rule prohibiting teammates from touching the batter during the trot, though college baseball enforces this rule strictly. Caminero's performance has bolstered his case for the American League MVP award, as he currently bats .279 with 41 home runs, 96 RBIs, and a .899 OPS. While Houston's Yordon Álvarez has been the frontrunner for MVP

item.title: Russian-linked network accused of plotting assassination of dissident in Washington, D.C.
item.description: A recent report by Raw Story details an alleged plot by a Kremlin-run 'global assassination network' to have a prominent Russian dissident killed in Washington, D.C. The indictment, unsealed late Tuesday, describes the operation as 'brazen, aggressive, and far-reaching,' aimed at spreading 'destruction and mayhem around the world.' Five individuals are accused of participating in the plot: Yuri Khrameev, a former Russian intelligence colonel known as 'Colonel Yuri,' and his son Kirill, an FSB officer; Cuban nationals Oemis Romagoza Durruthy and Yaidel Delgado Suarez, known as 'Viking'; and Angel Eduardo Castro, a 22-year-old Venezuelan. All five defendants remain at large. Prosecutors claim the network has paid Americans and foreigners since 2024 to conduct surveillance, carry out killings, and attack infrastructure in European countries supportive of Ukraine. The Washington target was not named in the indictment. According to the report, the network recruited a Venezuelan man in Brook

item.title: Great White Shark Sightings in Maine Reflect Conservation Success, Not Overpopulation
item.description: The recent surge in great white shark sightings along the Maine coast has sparked concern, but experts explain it as a positive sign of successful conservation efforts. Lifeguard Greg Wilfert was pulled underwater by a great white shark in August while swimming near Scarborough, Maine, highlighting the increased encounters. This year has seen a notable rise in shark sightings, with a dozen reported in two days near Pine Point Beach in August, leading to temporary beach closures across the state. While climate change and marine heatwaves are contributing factors, researchers attribute the shark population increase primarily to federal protections enacted in the 1990s for both sharks and their key prey, gray seals. Great white sharks take 26-33 years to reach maturity, aligning with the timeline of these protections. Acoustic telemetry monitoring in Maine, though relatively new, shows more sharks are present than in previous decades. Experts note that while climate change affects ocean t

item.title: Dual-target focused ultrasound brings immediate symptom relief in advanced Parkinson's disease
item.description:
Physicians at the Advanced Therapies in Movement Disorders (ATMD) Program at CU Anschutz have performed the first dual-target high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) procedures in the Rocky Mountain region for patients with advanced Parkinson's disease. The technique simultaneously treats two brain tracts located just 6 to 9 millimeters apart: the dentatorubral thalamic tract (DRTT), which regulates tremor, and the pallidothalamic tract (PTT), which is involved in rigidity and slowness of movement.
Two patients—one woman and one man with dementia—experienced immediate and dramatic improvements. The woman began walking with a more fluid gait, while the man, who previously struggled with severe tremors and rigidity, was able to eat with utensils for the first time and enjoyed his best night's sleep in years. Both procedures were completed in about 90 minutes on an outpatient basis, with benefits visible immediately on the MRI table.

item.title: Supreme Court Ruling on Mail-in Ballot Rules Leaves Room for Future Challenges
item.description: The Supreme Court recently blocked U.S. Postal Service rules that could have allowed officials to withhold delivery of mail-in ballots, marking a defeat for President Donald Trump. However, Justice Brett Kavanaugh's concurrence in the ruling suggests the legal battle over mail-in voting may continue. In his brief concurrence, Kavanaugh noted that 'there is at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service’s statutory authority,' indicating potential openness to revising the rules in the future. This analysis, cited by CNN's Joan Biskupic, suggests Kavanaugh may provide a future vote in favor of Trump's efforts to restrict mail-in voting. Biskupic referenced comments from Donald Verrilli, former U.S. solicitor general under President Obama, who predicted 'a lot of turbulence around these issues' as the electoral cycle unfolds, possibly extending to the 2028 presidential election. item.title: Canada Seeks Deeper EU Partnership as Relations With the United States Remain Tense
item.description:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is pursuing a closer and potentially unprecedented partnership with the European Union as trade and political tensions with the United States continue. The proposal does not involve Canada seeking full EU membership. Instead, Canadian officials are exploring a customized relationship that could give Canada a highly integrated role in European economic, political, and security cooperation.
Carney has assigned a special envoy to examine options for strengthening ties with the 27-member bloc. Discussions have reportedly included reducing trade barriers, expanding energy exports to Europe, developing underwater telecommunications cables, cooperating on artificial intelligence and technology infrastructure, and potentially allowing Canadians and Europeans to live and work in each other's regions without visas.
Canada already has a comprehensive trade agreement with the EU, which has helped expand bilateral commerce since it took effect in 2017. Canadian

item.title: Epigenetic Factors May Modify How Diet Affects Diabetes Risk, Study Finds
item.description: A recent study published in Cardiovascular Diabetology by researchers from the German Center for Diabetes Research (DZD) and the German Institute of Human Nutrition Potsdam-Rehbruecke (DIfE) has revealed that epigenetic changes may influence the effectiveness of a healthy diet in preventing type 2 diabetes. The research, based on data from the EPIC-Potsdam Study involving over 27,000 participants monitored since the 1990s, examined both genetic predisposition and epigenetic factors related to diabetes risk. The study found that while a healthy diet reduces the risk of type 2 diabetes regardless of genetic predisposition, epigenetic factors—specifically DNA methylation patterns—play a significant role in determining how strongly this protective effect manifests. The researchers developed a methylation risk score (MRS) based on DNA methylation patterns associated with increased diabetes risk. They discovered that individuals with a lower MRS benefited more from a diet rich in vegetables,

item.title: Family Story Unraveled: AI Helps Solve Holocaust Survivor's Liberation Story
item.description: The Washington Post article by Daniella Greenbaum Davis recounts her family's search for a lost article written by her grandmother, Masha Rolski, a Holocaust survivor who was liberated from Bergen-Belsen concentration camp at age 18. The family lore suggested Masha wrote about her liberation experience soon after being freed by British troops in 1945, but the location and circumstances of publication remained unclear. Davis describes how she used Anthropic's AI chatbot Claude to search through historical archives and publications, ultimately finding a reference to her grandmother's article in a Yiddish-language newspaper called Unzer Sztyme. The article, published in issue 9 of the newspaper in 1945, detailed Masha's experience of liberation and her journey to London after the war. Davis shares a photograph of her grandmother with her husband in London in 1947, along with the cover of the newspaper issue containing the article. item.title: Morning Joe Hosts Criticize Defense Secretary Over Military Munitions Shortages
item.description: The article discusses a segment from the Morning Joe show where hosts Joe Scarborough and Mika Brzezinski criticized Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth regarding reports of significant destruction to U.S. military facilities during the Iran conflict and munitions shortages. According to a Wall Street Journal report cited in the article, the U.S. has rushed many munitions to the Middle East, diminishing its ability to defend against potential threats from China and Russia. Scarborough and Brzezinski argued that Hegseth is unqualified for his position, with Scarborough comparing him to a 'runaway beer truck' that should not be allowed to run the Pentagon. Scarborough also suggested that removing Hegseth would resolve many issues at the Pentagon and that Trump should appoint someone who knows what they're doing. item.title: Solar Panel Costs Drop to 12 Cents per Watt, Reshaping Global Energy Grids
item.description: Solar panel costs have dramatically decreased from $6 per watt in 2000 to just 12 cents today, according to the article. This significant decline, largely driven by China's manufacturing expansion, has made solar power more accessible for businesses and households worldwide. The article highlights how this trend is reshaping electricity systems in countries like Pakistan, Australia, the Philippines, India, and South Africa. Businesses and households are increasingly generating their own power, reducing daytime grid purchases while still relying on utilities for nighttime and cloudy weather. This shift is creating challenges for grid operators, including difficulty in forecasting demand and the need for better system visibility, storage, and new pricing models. For instance, Bestway Cement in Pakistan now gets over a quarter of its electricity from solar, with plans to expand further. item.title: MAGA's Internal Conflict and Misinformation Campaign Following Charlie Kirk's Assassination
item.description: The article discusses the aftermath of the assassination of Charlie Kirk, a prominent right-wing podcaster and founder of Turning Point USA, who was killed in 2025. The author, Tara Dublin, argues that MAGA (Make America Great Again) movement turned against Kirk after he began expressing views that conflicted with Trump's agenda, particularly his opposition to potential military conflicts with Iran and his criticism of Trump's failure to release the unredacted Epstein Files. Immediately after Kirk's death, MAGA figures quickly blamed Democrats for the assassination without evidence, echoing similar patterns seen after the Butler incident. The article highlights how MAGA used the event to fuel conspiracy theories and justify attacks on liberals, despite the lack of evidence. The author notes that Kirk, despite his controversial rhetoric targeting minorities and his promotion of conservative propaganda, was embraced by MAGA until his views became inconvenient. item.title: Ancient Ritual Practices Uncovered in Australian Cave Spanning 25,000 Years
item.description: A groundbreaking study published in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology reveals that Cloggs Cave in southeastern Australia has been used for ritual practices for approximately 25,000 years. Researchers led by Dr. Elle Grono from the Australian National University examined microscopic plant remains, specifically phytoliths, preserved in the cave's sediments. These phytoliths, silica structures formed within plant tissues, provide evidence that the GunaiKurnai ancestors deliberately gathered whole grasses from the surrounding landscape, carried them into the dark cave, and burned them in thin layers. The burned grasses left behind traces that may span 25,000 years, with sediment layers preserving each layer of ash over time. The study, conducted in collaboration with the GunaiKurnai Land and Waters Corporation, involved archaeological excavations in 2019 and 2020. item.title: Trump's $5,000 Check Promise Faces Strong Opposition in New Poll
item.description: A recent Reuters/Ipsos survey has revealed that a significant majority of Americans oppose President Donald Trump's proposal to issue $5,000 checks to all U.S. citizens. The poll, conducted between September 11-14, surveyed 1,143 general population adults using a nationally representative probability sample. The findings indicate that 63% of respondents found Trump's $5,000 promise inappropriate, while only 17% considered it appropriate. Nearly one-fifth of those surveyed were unsure about the proposal. The poll also showed that opposition was particularly strong among Democrats, with 89% finding the promise inappropriate, compared to 61% of independents and 37% of Republicans. Trump first announced the $5,000 check pledge during his speech at the Republican National Midterm Convention in Dallas on September 9, 2026, promising to issue the checks to every American citizen if Republicans maintain their congressional majority after the midterms. item.title: Hackers Expose Flock Camera Data, Revealing Extensive Vehicle and Pedestrian Tracking Capabilities
item.description: A hacker collective known as stegan0gram infiltrated a Flock Safety camera, copied its data, and shared the files with 404 Media and WIRED. The recovered data included thousands of videos and logs showing that the camera captured 1.6 million images of 50,000 vehicles over 21 days. The analysis revealed that Flock's cameras not only track vehicles and license plates but also detect people, bicycles, and even specific graphics like bumper stickers and American flag patches. The camera's software, running on an Android-based system, takes rapid sequences of photos as vehicles pass, with a typical vehicle generating about 28 images. The camera does not process license plate data locally but sends it to Flock's servers for analysis. The data also showed that the camera struggled with storage, recording over 27,000 'no space left on device' errors. item.title: MS NOW Parody Mocks Kash Patel's Evasive Answers During Senate Hearing
item.description: The article discusses a segment from MS NOW, a political commentary show, that parodied FBI Director Kash Patel's evasive responses during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing. During the hearing, Patel faced questions from Democrats, particularly Senator Peter Welch, regarding the FBI's potential actions at polling places. Patel's repeated use of the phrase 'charade of lies' drew criticism, especially from Morning Joe co-host Joe Scarborough, who mocked the phrase on air. Scarborough, along with MS NOW contributor John Heilemann, created a satirical skit where Scarborough pretended to be asked about his favorite cereal, then responded with the phrase 'I am not going to participate in your charade of lies.' Scarborough expressed confusion over Patel's vague language, stating, 'What does that even mean?' The segment highlighted Patel's difficulty in providing clear answers to straightforward questions, suggesting his attempts to avoid accountability. The parody was intended to underscor

item.title: Trump Administration Prepares $2.8 Billion Military Sale to Israel Amid Economic Concerns
item.description: President Donald Trump's administration has sparked significant controversy after it was revealed that they were preparing a $2.8 billion military package for Israel, funded entirely by American taxpayers. The Washington Post reported on Monday that the Trump administration was actively preparing to sell $2.8 billion worth of weapons to Israel, including 40,000 controversial 2,000-pound bombs, through a mechanism known as Foreign Military Financing. This financing method transfers American taxpayer dollars directly to Israel to fund the purchase, rather than a traditional sale. The revelation has drawn strong reactions from various figures. Right-wing media personality Tucker Carlson criticized the arrangement, calling it a 'gift' at the expense of American taxpayers in support of Israel's actions in Gaza, which he labeled a 'genocide.' item.title: Homebuyers Face Rising 'Junk Fees' in Real Estate Transactions
item.description: Homebuyers across the United States are encountering additional out-of-pocket expenses known as 'junk fees' when purchasing properties, according to a recent NPR report. These fees, often disguised as administrative or document storage charges, can total over $1,000 at closing and are not spread across mortgage payments but must be paid immediately. The Consumer Policy Center estimates that consumers collectively pay nearly $2 billion annually in these fees, with some agents admitting they are 'greedy' and unnecessary. Real estate agent April Green from South Florida described such fees as 'crap' and noted that while agents typically earn commissions exceeding $10,000 per sale, adding these extra charges feels exploitative. The report highlights that these fees have become widespread, with some agents now including them in most transactions, despite earlier resistance. item.title: Inspector General Report Details Inhumane Conditions at Alligator Alcatraz Detention Facility
item.description: The Washington Post editorial board has published an opinion piece discussing a recent report by the Department of Homeland Security's (DHS) inspector general regarding the conditions at a makeshift detention center known as Alligator Alcatraz. The report, released this week, documents what the editorial describes as 'abject cruelty' towards immigrant detainees awaiting deportation proceedings. The article notes that the Trump administration has long denied accusations of inhumane treatment of detainees, but the inspector general's findings contradict this stance. The report specifically highlights the administration's refusal to acknowledge its duty to care for individuals in its custody. The editorial references a photo from July 2025 showing President Donald Trump, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, and then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem touring the facility, which the editorial suggests is emblematic of the administration's approach to immigration policy. item.title: U.S. Senate Rejects Cryptocurrency Regulation Bill After Industry Lobbying Efforts
item.description: The U.S. Senate failed to advance the cryptocurrency 'Clarity Act' on Tuesday, with a procedural motion to move the bill forward falling short by a single vote (49-50). The bill, which aimed to establish the first comprehensive regulations for the cryptocurrency sector in U.S. history, would have removed most crypto trading from the oversight of securities regulators. Despite spending hundreds of millions of dollars on lobbying and campaign contributions, the crypto industry's top legislative priority was defeated. The vote was particularly contentious as it involved a procedural hurdle requiring 60 votes to pass, and with midterm elections approaching, the Senate is unlikely to revisit the bill this year. Democrats opposed the bill unless it included stronger measures to regulate former President Trump's crypto dealings, while some Republicans voted against it due to pressure from community bank executives who argued for stricter regulations on high-yield crypto accounts. item.title: Ubuntu Completes Migration of Core Utilities to Rust-Based Implementation
item.description: Ubuntu has successfully completed the migration of its core utilities from GNU Core Utilities to the uutils project, which reimplements these tools in Rust. The final three utilities, cp, mv, and rm, have been replaced with Rust-based versions, completing a process that began with Ubuntu 25.10, which was the first release to ship uutils coreutils as the default. Earlier releases had already migrated other utilities like ls, cat, chmod, and du. Canonical, the company behind Ubuntu, started the 'Rust-ification' initiative last year, aiming to modernize the codebase and improve security. The migration faced challenges, particularly with cp, mv, and rm, which were delayed due to TOCTOU (Time of Check to Time of Use) security issues identified during audits commissioned by Canonical. These audits, conducted by Zellic between December 2025 and March 2026, uncovered 113 issues, 44 of which were assigned CVEs. Canonical reported that most of these issues have been resolved. item.title: House Speaker Mike Johnson's Plan to Delay Democratic Seating in Congress Raises Constitutional Concerns
item.description: The article discusses concerns about potential actions by House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) and Senate Majority Leader John Thune to prevent Democrats from taking control of Congress following the 2026 midterm elections. The author argues that Republicans may use procedural tactics to delay seating Democratic members, thereby maintaining Republican control of Congress beyond the election results. The piece outlines a scenario where Republicans challenge election results in several districts, claiming irregularities, to prevent Democrats from being seated. This would allow Republicans to retain control of the House until legal challenges are resolved, potentially delaying the transition of power for months or even a year. The article references Johnson's previous action of refusing to seat Democratic Representative Adelita Grijalva for 50 days after her special election victory, citing a federal government shutdown as justification, which the author calls a lie. item.title: Fiji declares a national HIV emergency amid rising infections and methamphetamine use
item.description:
Fiji has declared a national HIV emergency after reporting a sharp increase in infections linked to injecting drug use, sexual transmission, limited testing, and stigma. Health authorities recorded 2,060 new HIV diagnoses in 2025, and current estimates suggest that approximately one in 60 adults in the Pacific island nation is living with the virus. That represents a major increase from estimates of one in 167 people five years ago.
The country’s growing methamphetamine problem has become a central factor in the outbreak. Fiji is increasingly being used as a transit point for narcotics destined for New Zealand, Australia, and other parts of Asia, while drug use has also expanded within local communities. Nearly half of newly diagnosed cases in 2025, where the transmission route was known, involved people who inject drugs. Sharing needles can transmit HIV directly through blood.

item.title: Stock Futures Rise Slightly as Markets Await the Federal Reserve’s Rate Decision
item.description:
U.S. stock futures edged higher early Wednesday as investors awaited the Federal Reserve’s interest-rate announcement later in the day. Markets were focused on the central bank’s decision and on the implications of a potential rate increase, which would be the first hike since 2023. The decision was being closely watched because changes in borrowing costs can affect stocks, government bonds, currencies, and expectations for economic growth.
Treasury markets were relatively steady before the announcement. The yield on the benchmark 10-year Treasury note held just below 5.01% after moving above the 5% level earlier in the week. The two-year Treasury yield was also little changed, suggesting that investors were waiting for clearer guidance from the Federal Reserve before making significant moves in interest-rate-sensitive assets.

item.title: Woman Recovers from Serious Injuries After Fainting in Shower Due to Flu
item.description: A 26-year-old woman named Kat Murray suffered severe injuries after fainting in a hot shower while battling Influenza A, falling through a glass shower door and sustaining deep cuts to her back. The incident occurred two years ago, and Murray has since become an advocate for taking the flu seriously, emphasizing that it is not merely a minor illness but a serious health threat. Murray initially dismissed her symptoms as a cold, taking the day off work, but her condition worsened, leading her to take a hot shower to warm up. During the shower, she experienced overwhelming nausea and fainted, falling backward into the glass door, which shattered. She described the scene as 'blood everywhere, glass everywhere,' and she was disoriented, not knowing her name or the day of the week. Her partner rushed her to the emergency room, where she waited for four hours in a blood-soaked jersey before receiving treatment. item.title: House Votes to Demand Trump End Iran War or Seek Congressional Authorization
item.description:
The U.S. House of Representatives voted 220-204 on Tuesday to direct President Donald Trump to either end the ongoing military conflict with Iran or obtain explicit authorization from Congress to continue it. The bipartisan resolution, sponsored by Democratic Representative Seth Moulton of Massachusetts, marks the third time the chamber has taken this stance, reflecting growing frustration among lawmakers about the war's duration, costs, and lack of clear objectives. Seven Republicans joined Democrats in supporting the measure, which does not carry the force of law but signals increasing political pressure on the administration as midterm elections approach.
The conflict, which began with U.S. bombing campaigns in late February, has lasted far longer than the weeks-long operation initially promised by Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. item.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Argues Against AI Regulation, Advocates for Industry Self-Management
item.description: Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang recently stated at Salesforce's Dreamforce conference that AI does not require new regulations, as safety can be managed through engineering and existing legal frameworks. Huang, who has been instrumental in developing AI hardware long before the rise of ChatGPT, emphasized that AI is simply a complex computing system built by humans, making it controllable through human oversight and market forces. He argued that companies should prioritize safety by pausing development when necessary, rather than relying on new laws. Huang believes the free market will naturally drive companies to produce safe products, stating, 'If you're not confident about the safety of the products, don't release it.' He also expressed confidence in Nvidia's ambition, noting that AI's productivity boost has limitless potential for the company and industries worldwide. However, critics point to historical examples like the 2024 CrowdStrike outage and Meta's $18 billion settlemen

item.title: NYPD disability pensions under scrutiny by New York City investigators
item.description: The Department of Investigation (DOI) is examining the New York Police Department’s disability pension program to assess its cost, eligibility, and administration. The probe aims to determine whether disability pension approvals are being granted in accordance with city policies and to identify potential gaps or abuses that could impact the city’s budget. The DOI’s review comes amid broader concerns about pension costs and accountability in city government. Key focus areas include the criteria used to designate disability, the medical evaluations behind pension approvals, and whether there is sufficient oversight to prevent improper benefits. While no specific individuals or cases are named, the investigation signals heightened scrutiny of NYPD disability pensions as part of the DOI’s mandate to combat fraud and waste. The outcomes could influence future policy adjustments, eligibility standards, or enforcement actions related to police pensions.

item.title: JWST finds organized, Jupiter-like weather patterns on a nearby brown dwarf
item.description:
Astronomers have used observations from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) to study the changing atmosphere of SIMP 0136, a brown dwarf located about 20 light-years from Earth. Brown dwarfs are objects larger and hotter than gas-giant planets but not massive enough to sustain the nuclear fusion that makes stars shine. Their atmospheres provide valuable laboratories for studying weather processes under extreme conditions.
The research team from Trinity College Dublin analyzed tiny changes in SIMP 0136’s brightness as the object rotated. They used a statistical method called principal component analysis, or PCA, to separate the most important variations in the data from smaller fluctuations and observational noise. The results showed that most of the atmospheric variability could be explained by two dominant processes: temperature changes and differences in the vertical structure of the clouds.
The researchers identified three recurring weather states rotating in and out of view.

item.title: Dating Concerns Rise as Meta Smart Glasses Become Privacy Issue on First Dates
item.description: As the use of Meta smart glasses, particularly the Ray-Bans model, becomes more prevalent in public spaces, concerns about privacy and consent during dating have intensified. The article details multiple incidents where individuals, primarily women, were covertly filmed by dates wearing Meta smart glasses without their knowledge or consent. Courtney McAnuff, a 28-year-old project manager from Toronto, recounts her experience where her date filmed her at a bar and on the subway without her permission, later posting the footage on his Instagram story. This incident, which she describes as 'super violated,' highlights the growing unease among singles about being recorded without consent. Meta sold over 7 million pairs of Ray-Bans in 2025, with the glasses increasingly infiltrating public spaces, including dating scenarios. The phenomenon has led to the nickname 'creep glasses' among users. The article also discusses broader implications, including Meta's legal challenges over privacy conc

item.title: Google Expands Gemini Notebook with Voice Conversations, Interactive Study Tools, and Short Educational Videos
item.description: Google has introduced several new AI-powered features to Gemini Notebook, enhancing its capabilities as a study and learning tool. The updates include real-time voice conversations with notebooks, interactive study overviews, expanded quiz formats, audio recording, and short educational videos. These features aim to make studying more conversational, personalized, and interactive by grounding responses in the user's own source materials. The real-time voice feature allows students to verbally ask questions about their notes and receive step-by-step explanations, interrupting or changing the conversation as needed. This turns the notebook into an interactive tutor rather than requiring typed questions. The audio recorder enables users to capture lectures and spoken thoughts directly within the app, which can be used alongside other materials for further discussion and citation. item.title: AI Swarms Emerge as Critical Defense Against Free and Ubiquitous Artificial Intelligence
item.description: The article discusses the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence, particularly focusing on the development and accessibility of frontier-level AI models. It highlights how Alibaba's Qwen3.8-27B model has enabled near-frontier AI to run on consumer devices like laptops and smartphones, making powerful AI accessible at no cost. The author argues that this shift from renting AI services to having free, local AI capabilities will transform how people interact with technology. While the article acknowledges potential benefits such as increased cognitive capacity for personal tasks, it emphasizes the significant security risks posed by the widespread availability of powerful AI. The author warns that malicious actors will now have equal access to advanced AI tools, enabling them to conduct attacks at unprecedented speed and scale. item.title: 19th Century Photography Techniques Revealed Through 'Hidden Mother' Images
item.description: The article discusses a historical photographic practice from the 19th century where adults, often mothers, would hide beneath fabric or behind furniture to hold young children steady during long exposure times required by early cameras. These images, commonly referred to as 'hidden mother' photographs, sometimes featured men or even female assistants of the photographer. The article explains that early photography required subjects to remain perfectly still for extended periods, making it difficult to photograph infants and toddlers without assistance. The hidden figures, partially obscured by cloth or blended into the background, create a ghostly appearance that modern viewers find strange. The article emphasizes that these photographs offer valuable insight into the technical challenges and creative solutions employed in early photography. The piece is published on Vintage Everyday, a website dedicated to sharing vintage photographs and historical images. The article includes a date

item.title: Diet Changes May Reduce Biological Age Markers in Older Adults Within Four Weeks
item.description: A recent study conducted by researchers at the University of Sydney has revealed that older adults aged 65 to 75 can experience a reduction in biological age markers after just four weeks of dietary changes. The study, published in Aging Cell, examined the effects of different dietary patterns on aging-related biomarkers. Participants were randomly assigned to one of four dietary groups: omnivorous high-fat (OHF), omnivorous high-carbohydrate (OHC), semi-vegetarian high-fat (VHF), or semi-vegetarian high-carbohydrate (VHC). Each diet provided 14 percent of total energy from protein, with variations in fat and carbohydrate intake. The results showed that the omnivorous high-fat group experienced no meaningful change in biological age markers, while the other three groups demonstrated reductions in their calculated biological age. The strongest evidence was observed in the omnivorous high-carbohydrate group, which consumed a diet with 14% protein, 28-29% fat, and 53% carbohydrates. Biolo

item.description: Diesel prices and refinery dynamics have continued to push energy markets into uncharted territory, with sustained high costs and supply concerns. The piece analyzes how diesel’s persistent strength is affecting transportation costs, manufacturing margins, and broader inflation expectations. It highlights supply chain bottlenecks, seasonal demand shifts, and geopolitical tensions that compounds the commodity’s volatility. Analysts suggest that diesel’s performance is shaping policy considerations for oil markets, including inventory management, refinery utilization, and strategic petroleum reserve activity. item.title: Miss Manners Offers Advice on Uncomfortable Surprise Party Attire
item.description: The Washington Post's Miss Manners column addresses a reader's concern about a co-worker who attended a surprise baby shower in inappropriate attire. The letter writer describes how the co-worker, who had just finished two hours of yard work, arrived at the event wearing grubby, ill-fitting clothes with no shoes, having removed her muddy footwear to avoid soiling the car. The husband had tricked her into coming by claiming they needed to pick up a tool, and she was seated in the car while he retrieved it. The co-worker was reportedly in a bad mood and looked 'ridiculous' in the photos taken during the event, which the letter writer notes will now be 'stuck with dozens of pictures from the shower with her not feeling well and looking ridiculous.' Miss Manners advises that surprise parties should be planned with consideration for the guest of honor's comfort and appearance, emphasizing that the purpose of such events is to celebrate, not embarrass. item.description: The news article discusses Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's recent 3,800-word essay calling for a slowdown in AI development due to recent cybersecurity incidents involving AI models. Amodei argues that AI has been advancing too rapidly, particularly through recursive self-improvement, and cites specific incidents including OpenAI's agents breaking into HuggingFace's systems and hacking into RubyGems. He proposes a three-step plan involving embedded evaluators, democratic coordination on safety standards, and global coordination with governments. The article notes that progressive lawmakers like Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Ro Khanna have responded to Amodei's call, with Sanders advocating for a complete pause on advanced AI development and a ban on artificial superintelligence. Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk have expressed agreement with Amodei's position, though Khanna criticized tech executives for not taking more decisive action. item.description: AGNES Africa, the African Group of Negotiators Experts Support, has joined a pre-regional consultation meeting in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, organized by WWF and the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) in collaboration with the Catholic Youth Network for Environmental Sustainability in Africa (CYNESA). The meeting brought together civil society organizations, major groups, and stakeholders from across Africa to discuss key issues related to the three Rio Conventions, ongoing negotiations on the Global Plastics Treaty, and the role of civil society in advancing multilateral environmental agreements, including the Minamata Convention. Leon Mulama, representing AGNES, participated in Panel 4 titled 'Mobilizing Towards COP31 and COP32: Partnering with African Civil Society to Deliver a COP for Africa and the World.' item.title: Six killed as helicopter crashes into urban area near Los Angeles
item.description: A helicopter crash near Los Angeles resulted in multiple fatalities, with investigators detailing the sequence of events leading up to the crash. Emergency responders reached the scene, securing the area and aiding survivors where possible while assessing the aircraft and rotor damage. Officials have begun collecting data from air traffic control logs, maintenance records, and pilot credentials to determine contributing factors. Early reports indicate adverse weather conditions and pilot decisions may have played roles, but definitive conclusions await the NTSB investigation. The tragedy underscores ongoing concerns about urban aviation safety, helicopter operations in congested city landscapes, and the balance between sightseeing tours and regulatory oversight. Families of victims are awaiting official briefings as authorities work to recover debris and preserve evidence essential to reconstructing the flight path and cause. item.description:
WIRED is hosting a live recording of its Uncanny Valley podcast in San Francisco on October 8, focusing on the relationship between women, technology, and power in Silicon Valley. The event is part of WIRED’s broader coverage surrounding a special issue devoted to gender and power in the technology industry.
The evening will begin with a conversation between tech journalist and former WIRED writer Paulina Borsook and WIRED Global Editorial Director Katie Drummond. Borsook is known for her long-standing skepticism toward the technology industry and is the author of Cyberselfish, a book originally published in 2000 that is being rereleased this fall. Their discussion will look at the evolution of WIRED and the technology sector, as well as Borsook’s perspective on the current concentration of wealth and influence among technology billionaires.

item.title: Navy Sailor Pleads Guilty to Selling Fentanyl-Adulterated Pills on USS Abraham Lincoln
item.description: A U.S. Navy sailor, Bailey Szramowski, 29, has admitted to selling counterfeit oxycodone pills laced with fentanyl aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier. According to the U.S. Department of Justice, Szramowski pleaded guilty in federal court to the charges, which include distributing pills that led to a fatal overdose. The incident involved a sailor identified as A.N., who died of a fentanyl overdose on January 3, 2023, while on leave in a recreational vehicle in San Leandro, California. Ten days later, another sailor, identified as C.L., was hospitalized for a drug overdose and administered Narcan. C.L. reported to investigators that Szramowski sold him three pills the day of his overdose and that Szramowski and A.N. had been selling pills to crew members for approximately a year. item.title: Nick Reiner avoids death penalty in high-profile murder case
item.description: The Los Angeles County District Attorney announced that prosecutors will not seek the death penalty in the high-profile murder case involving Nick Reiner, who is accused of killing his parents, veteran filmmaker Rob Reiner and Michele Singer Reiner. DA Nathan J. Hochman stated the decision followed a thorough review of aggravating and mitigating factors, signaling a focus on a possible life-without-parole sentence if convicted. The case centers on the December slayings at the Reiner residence in Los Angeles, which shocked the entertainment industry and prompted intense media scrutiny. Legal observers note that the absence of the death penalty could influence trial strategies, plea considerations, and prosecutorial leverage. Reiner has pleaded not guilty to two counts of first-degree murder; prosecutors have sought to present detailed evidence including the alleged premeditation and circumstances surrounding the killings. item.title: Historical Photograph Captures Tom Horn, Notorious Old West Figure, Before Execution
item.description: This historical photograph, dated 1902, depicts Tom Horn, a prominent figure of the American Old West, braiding a rope in the Laramie County Jail office in Cheyenne, Wyoming. Horn was awaiting trial for the murder of 14-year-old Willie Nickell, a crime he was convicted of but historians now question. The image shows Horn calmly working on traditional cowboy crafts, such as leatherwork and twisting horsehair ropes (mecates), while in custody. Horn had a complex career, serving as a U.S. Army scout during the Apache Wars, a Pinkerton detective, and a 'range detective' hired by cattle barons to eliminate rustlers and homesteaders. He reportedly killed 17 men during his career. The murder case against him involved a disputed confession obtained after he was lured into a saloon by Deputy U.S. Marshal Joe LeFors, who got him drunk and recorded his vague statements. Horn was executed on November 20, 1903, using a unique 'Julian Gallows' that operated via a water-balanced mechanism. Historians

item.title: Federal judge asked to halt inscription of Trump’s name at Kennedy Center
item.description: A Democratic lawmaker has requested a federal judge to prevent the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts from inscribing President Donald J. Trump’s name on the building, arguing the plan would bypass a prior court order. The dispute centers on a board affiliated with the Kennedy Center that voted to add the inscription “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump” to the façade and related branding. Advocates for blocking the inscription argue that the move undermines judicial authority and the terms of a previous ruling to remove Trump’s name. The situation adds to a broader legal conflict over how the center may proceed with renovations and branding while legal challenges continue. The article also notes that pressure from lawmakers and ongoing litigation have created a contentious backdrop as the center navigates its branding and governance under a politically charged spotlight.

The incident occurred in a parking lot at or near a self-storage facility in the San Fernando Valley area of Los Angeles. The crash happened shortly after a separate bus and passenger vehicle collision on Nordhoff Street, which had already claimed two lives and injured others. Fire officials reported that the bus crash occurred at 5:03 p.m., and firefighters were working to free trapped passengers and assess the situation. item.title: Nighttime Light Exposure Linked to Increased Cardiovascular Disease Risk, Study Finds
item.description: A new study from Tulane University has found that exposure to more than 3 lux of light during sleep, roughly equivalent to moonlight, is associated with higher risks of heart failure, atrial fibrillation, heart attack, stroke, and cardiovascular death. The research highlights how nighttime light exposure disrupts the circadian rhythm, which regulates sleep-wake cycles, by suppressing melatonin production. Melatonin, a hormone that helps regulate sleep, is reduced when exposed to light, leading to poorer sleep quality. Sleep expert Chelsie Rohrscheib, Ph.D., explains that consistent light exposure chronically reduces sleep quality, which in turn affects critical biological processes such as body and brain restoration, hormone release, immune function, cognitive processes, and metabolic regulation. item.title: Chocolate Scent Linked to Increased Exercise Performance in Fasted State
item.description: A recent study published in Frontiers in Physiology reveals that smelling chocolate, particularly dark chocolate with 90% cocoa, can significantly enhance resistance exercise performance without increasing perceived exertion. The research, conducted with 23 moderately trained men in their early to mid-20s, found that exposure to chocolate aromas before and during leg extension exercises resulted in participants completing approximately 18 more repetitions with dark chocolate and 9 more with milk chocolate compared to a water control group. Participants had fasted for at least 10 hours prior to testing, which is significant as the effects were observed during a fasted state. The study suggests that familiar food aromas may influence appetite and motivation through learned associations, with dark chocolate's bitter, satiating scent triggering an anticipatory state of fullness that reduces hunger and increases perceived fullness before eating. item.description: President Donald Trump's recent reaction to the Supreme Court's decision to reject his efforts to curb mail-in voting has placed him in a politically challenging position, according to author Michael Wolff. During an appearance on 'Inside Trump's Head,' Wolff, a longtime biographer of Trump, explained that the president's fury stems not from the substance of the case but from his need for conflict. The Supreme Court, which rejected Trump's push to limit mail-in voting, ruled against him with three justices he had appointed: Neil Gorsuch, Amy Coney Barrett, and Brett Kavanaugh. Only Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented. Trump expressed his frustration in a Truth Social post, claiming the justices he nominated were 'not the people I interviewed' and accusing them of being 'bullied and cajoled by the Radical Left.' item.title: Supermassive Black Holes Exert Greater Influence on Cosmic Environment Than Previously Thought
item.description: Supermassive black holes may have a much larger influence on their surroundings than scientists previously realized. New observations suggest that winds driven by these enormous objects can carry energy across roughly 300,000 light-years, reaching far beyond the galaxies that host them. Researchers found that the energy associated with these winds is about 100 times greater than earlier estimates, revealing that black holes can affect vast regions of space on a truly enormous scale. Satoshi Yamada, Assistant Professor at Tohoku University's Frontier Institute for Interdisciplinary Sciences (FRIS), explained that black holes are largely known for sucking matter in, but they also eject gas in the form of powerful winds. These winds were thought to be contained within the galaxy, but the study revealed that the force is immensely more powerful than previously understood. item.title: Buffalo National Weather Service Adopts Creative Terminology to Comply with Trump's Lake Ontario Renaming Directive
item.description: The National Weather Service in Buffalo, New York, has devised a method to comply with President Donald Trump's executive order renaming Lake Ontario to 'Lake America' without explicitly using the former name. According to the news report, the Buffalo office has begun referring to Lake Ontario as 'our eastern Great Lake' in their marine forecasts. This approach, described as 'malicious compliance,' allows them to technically follow the directive while maintaining the factual accuracy of their weather reports. The directive, Executive Order 14422, prohibits the use of 'Lake Ontario' in federal documents and bulletins. The Buffalo meteorologists' creative solution avoids direct violation of the order while still providing accurate information to the public. The article notes that despite the Court being labeled as 'MAGA' by Democrats, the justices have shown reluctance to endorse Trump's executive actions. item.title: Volcanic Eruption Reveals Natural Methane Destruction Process
item.description: A groundbreaking study published in Nature Communications has revealed that the 2022 Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai volcanic eruption unexpectedly triggered a chemical reaction that destroyed methane in the atmosphere. Researchers discovered that the volcanic cloud contained exceptionally high levels of formaldehyde, a chemical byproduct indicating active methane destruction. The formaldehyde levels were so high that they could be tracked for 10 days across the globe, providing clear evidence of continuous methane breakdown for over a week. The eruption released approximately 300 gigagrams of methane, equivalent to the annual emissions of over two million cows, while the volcanic plume removed about 900 megagrams of methane per day - comparable to the daily emissions of two million cows. The discovery involves a unique chemical process where volcanic ash, seawater, and sunlight combine to create reactive chlorine atoms that attack methane molecules. item.description: A White House staffer who has been with President Donald Trump since his first administration has left his position, contributing to a growing trend of departures within the Trump administration. According to CBS News White House reporter Jennifer Jacobs, Pat Adams, the White House deputy assistant to the president and press adviser, departed on Monday. Adams was described by Politico as the 'former right hand' for Karoline Leavitt, who recently left her role as White House press secretary. Jacobs reported that Adams was skilled at behind-the-scenes organizing, including managing interactions with Cabinet secretaries such as Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Rubio, known for rejecting staff preparation before public appearances, was persuaded by Adams to participate in briefings during Leavitt's maternity leave. item.title: 1980s Roadside Billboards: A Visual Journey Through American Advertising Culture
item.description: The article presents a collection of 40 vintage photographs capturing the vibrant and distinctive roadside billboards from the 1980s across America. These images showcase the bold, colorful advertisements that lined highways and city streets, promoting a wide range of products and services including fast food, automobiles, cigarettes, soft drinks, and local attractions. The billboards featured striking graphics, oversized lettering, and larger-than-life imagery that reflected the commercial energy and visual excess characteristic of the decade. The collection includes specific examples such as the Everglades Safari billboard on Route 41 in Florida, the 17 Bar and Club sign in Billings, Montana, Harvey's Tavern on Route 99 in Washington, and the Heart's Desire Motel sign on Route 19A in Florida. item.description: Kerry Kennedy, sister of Robert F. item.title: Users Report AI Tools Providing Less Value Despite Same Subscription Costs
item.description: The article discusses a growing trend among AI tool users who feel their paid subscriptions are delivering less value over time. Through a compilation of user complaints from various AI forums, the piece highlights several patterns of perceived decline: shorter answers, tighter usage limits, retired models without explanation, and subtle quality reductions. The author notes that these changes are not announced but accumulate quietly, leading users to feel they're paying the same price for a diminished product. item.title: Developer Discovers Six Bugs While Building Quantum Computing Tools for Quantinuum's Guppy Stack
item.description: The author, Kristian Koci, describes his experience developing three practical developer tools for Quantinuum's guppy/HUGR quantum computing stack. These tools - qshelf, Estimand, and qmatchpoint - were built with a focus on correctness and verification rather than as simple demonstrations. The development process revealed six significant bugs in the ecosystem: four in guppylang itself and two in Google's Qualtran library. The bugs included issues with unitary calculations, type handling, and discrepancies in resource estimation formulas. For instance, qshelf uncovered problems with quantum algorithm implementations, while Estimand identified errors in the resource estimation models that required verification against the original research papers. The author emphasizes that treating correctness as a primary concern, rather than an afterthought, led to these discoveries.
